editorial / stablecoins & confidentiality

confidentiality is
the missing layer.

stablecoins are becoming payment infrastructure. the next question is who gets to see the payment.

by ems · @bringtheprofits

expanded from my original x article, published 2 january 2026. technical and policy details have been checked against primary sources; the analysis below is my interpretation.

stablecoins went really global in 2025. the conversation moved beyond trading and into something much more ordinary: how people and businesses move money.

that shift matters. once a payment becomes part of somebody’s working day, the expectations change. it has to arrive, it has to be usable, and it should not turn their finances into public content.

this was the point of my original post. adoption gets stablecoins into the room. confidentiality helps them belong there.

from a crypto thing to payment infrastructure

there was a concrete example near the end of 2025. visa announced that cross river bank and lead bank had begun settling with it in usdc on solana. the announcement described seven-day settlement without changing the consumer card experience. [1]

that is worth sitting with. a person can make an ordinary card payment while the institutions behind it change how they settle their obligations. adoption does not always arrive as a new app or a wallet everybody suddenly has to learn.

it can happen in the background.

this does not mean stablecoins replaced global payments in one year. it means we have specific examples of them becoming part of existing financial operations. that is a stronger argument than treating every announcement as proof that the whole world has already switched.

real payments come with real expectations

a payroll team is not trying to make an interesting blockchain transaction. it is trying to pay people correctly, on time, with records it can reconcile.

a business sending money to a supplier needs to know what arrived, what it cost, and who can resolve a problem. a person sending money home cares about whether the recipient can actually use it.

fast settlement is useful. so are reliable redemption, access to local money, sensible fees, and support when something goes wrong. confidentiality belongs alongside those requirements.

because a payment is also information.

your salary should not become a public dashboard

on a transparent public ledger, transfers can expose addresses, amounts, and patterns of activity. an address does not automatically tell you somebody’s name. but once the connection is known, a payment history can reveal much more than the sender intended.

think about payroll

imagine a company paying the same set of wallets every month. if those wallets become associated with employees, the amounts can reveal salary differences, bonuses, and changes in staffing.

the company wanted to pay its team. it did not set out to publish a compensation report.

the same issue appears with supplier payments and treasury movements. ordinary operational records can become clues about pricing, relationships, or business activity.

not every blockchain exposes the same information, and not every payment needs the same protection. but expecting businesses to accept unnecessary exposure as the price of using public infrastructure is a weak proposition.

the question becomes simple: who actually needs to see this?

transparency has an audience

a customer may need confidence in a stablecoin’s backing. a finance team needs payment records. an auditor may need access to evidence. the public does not necessarily need the details of every individual payment to satisfy those different needs.

in the united states, the genius act was enacted on 18 july 2025. its text establishes requirements including at least one-to-one eligible reserves, redemption-policy disclosures, monthly reserve reporting, and anti-money-laundering obligations. it also provides a staged effective-date mechanism rather than making enactment day the start of every requirement. [2]

that is a specific u.s. framework, not one global rulebook. and a confidentiality product does not become legally compliant just by calling itself compliant.

my point is about the design: protecting customer information and allowing appropriate oversight are both requirements worth building for. publishing everything to everybody is a very blunt way to approach that problem.

private by default, verifiable when needed

this remains the line i care about most from the original post.

the goal is controlled access to the right information. a recipient needs to understand their payment. an authorized reviewer needs relevant evidence. neither necessarily needs unrestricted visibility into somebody’s entire financial history.

selective disclosure is useful here. but the phrase only becomes meaningful when the rules are clear. who can authorize access? what records are included? can access be limited to a particular review? how is that decision recorded?

there is a difference between saying information is private and explaining precisely who can decrypt it.

where fairblock fits

fairblock is the project i highlighted because it is working on this layer. its current documentation describes confidential transfers with encrypted amounts and balances, while addresses remain visible in the standard model. it distinguishes that confidentiality from optional unlinkability. [3]

that distinction matters. hiding an amount is not the same as hiding every relationship around the transaction. privacy has a scope, and the scope should be understandable before anybody depends on it.

the documentation also describes stabletrust as its stablecoin product family, with tools for applications to integrate confidential transfers and a dashboard for scoped review by approved parties. these are the project’s descriptions of its capabilities, not an independent guarantee of security or regulatory acceptance. [3]

what interests me is the direction: give payment applications a way to protect sensitive values while retaining defined access for oversight. the useful outcome is a payment workflow people can understand and operate.

confidentiality has to survive the whole payment

encrypting a transfer amount is one part of the job. the surrounding application also matters.

if a payroll export, notification, or support dashboard exposes the same information to the wrong audience, the user still has a privacy problem. the experience needs to protect data across the places people actually work, not only inside one transaction.

and confidentiality cannot solve every other payment risk. it does not establish the quality of a stablecoin’s reserves, guarantee redemption, or repair a vulnerable contract. those questions still need their own answers.

for me, that makes confidentiality a requirement to evaluate seriously, not a label that ends the evaluation.

the missing layer

stablecoins have to work for the people using them, including people who do not want their salary, supplier terms, or business finances broadcast.

my argument is not that transparent payments are impossible. it is that unnecessary public exposure makes too many everyday uses harder than they need to be.

as more financial activity moves onchain, control over who can see what becomes part of the product itself.

move the money.
protect the details.
make the right things verifiable.

that is why i still see confidential stablecoins as a missing layer.

sources & editorial notes

expanded from my 2 january 2026 post. primary sources checked on 21 october 2026. the examples distinguish a documented payment rollout, enacted legislation, and fairblock’s own product descriptions. the argument for confidentiality is my analysis.

  1. visa — u.s. stablecoin settlement announcement, december 2025.
  2. u.s. government publishing office — genius act, sections 4 and 20.
  3. fairblock — confidential transfers documentation.
